name: Soma Cartography: Poems for New Bodies
creator: Rémy Nakashima-Diallo
description: A 94-poem collection exploring the phenomenology of augmented embodiment — what it feels like to have a chrome arm remember a lover's touch differently than a flesh one, or to experience grief through a BCI emotional filter set to 'managed.' Originally composed as a neural-feed sequence with embedded haptic pulses and subvocal tones, it was later transcribed to physical form by the poet, who insists the physical version is a 'translation, not a reproduction.' The two versions diverge meaningfully in the final third.
medium: licensed neural feed and limited physical edition (Nakashima-Diallo Press, 1,200 copies)
cultural_impact: Widely taught in Tier 3 and 4 educational institutions and credited with legitimizing augmentation-phenomenology as a poetic subject; the haptic neural version is considered one of the first genuinely new art forms native to BCI culture.
controversy: The Augmentation Workers Coalition objected that the collection aestheticizes chrome poverty — that Nakashima-Diallo, a Tier 4 resident with elective augments, romanticizes the experience of people who were chromed out of economic necessity.
story_hooks: A collector has discovered that copies 001 through 012 of the physical edition contain a poem not present in any other version, and the poet denies it exists.
A the Gray Zone community is using pirated haptic versions of the collection as a form of trauma therapy for involuntary augmentation survivors, drawing corporate legal attention.
The neural feed version has begun behaving anomalously in users with certain BCI architectures — generating new lines that no one wrote.
